question: Which ruler of the Gahadavala dynasty was defeated by Muhammad Ghori at the Battle of Chandawar in 1194?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Jaichandra.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Jaichandra, the Gahadavala ruler of Kannauj and Banaras, was defeated and killed by Muhammad Ghori at the Battle of Chandawar in 1194, near Firozabad on the Yamuna. (चंदावर का युद्ध — 1194)

 

• The battle came two years after the Second Battle of Tarain (1192), in which Ghori had defeated Prithviraj Chauhan. Between them the two victories destroyed the last substantial Rajput resistance in the Ganga valley and opened northern India to Turkish rule.

 

• Jaichandra is remembered in later tradition as the rival of Prithviraj Chauhan, and in the ballad literature as having failed to make common cause against the invader — which is why his name became a byword for treachery, though the historical evidence for it is thin.

 

• The Gahadavalas ruled from Kannauj, and it was under Govindachandra, Jaichandra's grandfather, that the dynasty was at its height.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Muhammad Ghori's campaigns in India:

 

• 1178 – defeated by Bhima II of Gujarat at Kayadara — his only major reverse

 

• 1191 – First Battle of Tarain; defeated by Prithviraj Chauhan

 

• 1192 – Second Battle of Tarain; defeated Prithviraj

 

• 1194 – Battle of Chandawar; defeated Jaichandra

 

• Ghori left his Indian conquests to his slave Qutb-ud-din Aibak, who founded the Slave dynasty in 1206 — the beginning of the Delhi Sultanate.

 

NOTE

 

• Govindachandra (Option 2): The greatest ruler of the Gahadavalas, and Jaichandra's grandfather, under whom the kingdom reached its widest extent. He is the strongest distractor.

 

• Vijaychandra (Option 3): Jaichandra's father, a lesser figure of the same line.

 

• Madanapala (Option 4): An earlier Gahadavala ruler, and the father of Govindachandra.

question: The Indian Institute of Science at Bengaluru was founded chiefly through the initiative and endowment of _____.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Jamsetji Tata.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Indian Institute of Science (IISc), Bengaluru, was founded chiefly through the initiative and endowment of Jamsetji Nusserwanji Tata, the founder of the Tata group. (भारतीय विज्ञान संस्थान — जमशेदजी टाटा)

 

• He conceived the idea in the 1890s, and set aside a large part of his personal fortune for it. The institute was established by a vesting order in 1909 and began teaching in 1911.

 

• It was a joint enterprise: the Tata endowment, land given by the Maharaja of Mysore, Krishnaraja Wadiyar IV, and the assent of the Government of India.

 

• Jamsetji did not live to see it — he died in 1904, five years before the institute was constituted.

 

• It is often called the "Tata Institute" for this reason, and has been ranked the foremost research institution in India for many years.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Jamsetji Tata's four stated ambitions were an iron and steel works, a world-class institution of learning, a hydro-electric plant and a great hotel. He saw only the last of them completed in his lifetime — the Taj Mahal Hotel, Bombay, 1903.

 

• Institutions and their founders:

 

• IISc, Bengaluru (1909) – Jamsetji Tata

 

• TIFR, Mumbai (1945) – Homi J. Bhabha, with Tata support

 

• IIT Kharagpur (1951) – the first IIT, on the recommendation of the Sarkar Committee

 

• CSIR (1942) and ICAR (1929)

 

NOTE

 

• J.R.D. Tata (Option 1): The great-nephew of Jamsetji, who headed the group from 1938 to 1991, founded Tata Airlines (later Air India) and helped establish TIFR and the Tata Memorial Hospital. He belongs to a later generation, which makes him the closest distractor.

 

• Homi J. Bhabha (Option 2): The father of India's nuclear programme, founder of TIFR (1945) and the first chairman of the Atomic Energy Commission.

 

• C.V. Raman (Option 4): Nobel laureate in Physics (1930) and the first Indian Director of IISc (1933) — but a director of the institute, not its founder.

question: Which of the following gives the correct chronological order (earliest to latest) of these rulers of the Delhi Sultanate?
option_1: Alauddin Khalji, Jalaluddin Khalji, Muhammad bin Tughlaq, Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq
option_2: Jalaluddin Khalji, Alauddin Khalji, Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq, Muhammad bin Tughlaq
option_3: Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq, Jalaluddin Khalji, Alauddin Khalji, Muhammad bin Tughlaq
option_4: Jalaluddin Khalji, Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq, Alauddin Khalji, Muhammad bin Tughlaq
solution_text:
The correct answer is Jalaluddin Khalji, Alauddin Khalji, Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq, Muhammad bin Tughlaq.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct order, with the years of accession, is: (दिल्ली सल्तनत — कालक्रम)

 

• Jalaluddin Khalji – 1290; founder of the Khalji dynasty, who came to the throne at about seventy and was noted for his mildness

 

• Alauddin Khalji – 1296; his nephew and son-in-law, who murdered him at Kara and seized the throne

 

• Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq – 1320; founder of the Tughlaq dynasty, formerly Ghazi Malik

 

• Muhammad bin Tughlaq – 1325; his son

 

• The two dynasties therefore follow one another without overlap, and within each the founder precedes his successor. Any option that reverses either pair is wrong.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Alauddin Khalji (1296-1316) is remembered for his market regulations and price control, for paying his soldiers in cash, for measuring land and fixing revenue at 50% of the produce, and for repelling repeated Mongol invasions. His generals Malik Kafur and Ulugh Khan carried Sultanate arms into the Deccan.

 

• Muhammad bin Tughlaq (1325-51) is remembered for two experiments that failed: the transfer of the capital to Daulatabad, and the issue of a token currency in brass and copper which was widely forged. Ibn Battuta visited his court and served as a judge.

 

• Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq built the fortress city of Tughlaqabad, and died when a pavilion collapsed on him in 1325.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 reverses the Khalji pair, putting Alauddin before his uncle Jalaluddin, and also reverses the Tughlaq pair.

 

• Option 3 places Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq first of all, thirty years before the dynasty he founded came to power.

 

• Option 4 inserts Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq between the two Khaljis, so that the dynasties are interleaved instead of following one another.

question: The Twenty Point Programme, aimed at the removal of poverty and the improvement of the quality of life, was first launched in India in which year?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1975.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Twenty Point Programme (TPP) was first launched on 1 July 1975 by Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. (बीस सूत्री कार्यक्रम — 1975)

 

• It was announced shortly after the declaration of the Emergency in June 1975, and its stated purpose was the eradication of poverty and the improvement of the quality of life of the poor and the underprivileged.

 

• Its measures covered land reform, the abolition of bonded labour, relief from rural indebtedness, minimum wages for agricultural labour, housing for the landless, and the extension of irrigation, drinking water and electricity.

 

• It has been restructured three times — in 1982, 1986 and 2006. The present version, TPP-2006, is monitored by the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The programme was launched during the Fifth Five Year Plan (1974-79), whose own slogan was "Garibi Hatao" — the removal of poverty — and the two were closely associated.

 

• Other landmarks of the same period:

 

• 1969 – nationalisation of 14 major banks

 

• 1971 – the slogan *Garibi Hatao* used in the general election

 

• 1980 – nationalisation of 6 more banks; launch of the Sixth Five Year Plan

 

NOTE

 

• 1969 (Option 1): The year fourteen banks were nationalised, and the year the Fourth Five Year Plan began. A landmark year, but not for this programme.

 

• 1980 (Option 3): The year the programme was in operation and being reviewed, and the year of the second round of bank nationalisation — but the first launch was five years earlier.

 

• 1991 (Option 4): The year of the New Economic Policy and the LPG reforms, which moved economic policy in an entirely different direction.

question: The "Ten Degree Channel" separates which two groups of islands?
option_1: The Andaman and the Nicobar Islands
option_4: The Amindivi and the Laccadive groups
solution_text:
The correct answer is The Andaman and the Nicobar Islands.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Ten Degree Channel separates the ANDAMAN group of islands from the NICOBAR group. (10 डिग्री चैनल — अंडमान एवं निकोबार के बीच)

 

• It takes its name from the fact that it lies almost exactly along the 10° North line of latitude.

 

• It is about 150 km wide and roughly 800 metres deep, and is one of the busiest shipping lanes in the region, carrying traffic between the Bay of Bengal and the Strait of Malacca.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Channels and straits of India, and what each separates — a set examined constantly:

 

• Ten Degree Channel – Andaman from Nicobar

 

• Nine Degree Channel – Lakshadweep from Minicoy

 

• Eight Degree Channel – Minicoy from the Maldives

 

• Palk Strait and the Gulf of Mannar – India from Sri Lanka, separated by Adam's Bridge (Ram Setu)

 

• Duncan Passage – South Andaman from Little Andaman

 

• Coco Strait – the Andamans from the Coco Islands of Myanmar

 

• Indira Point, on Great Nicobar, is the southernmost point of India.

 

NOTE

 

• The Lakshadweep and the Maldives (Option 2): Separated by the Eight Degree Channel, with Minicoy lying between them.

 

• Sumatra and Java (Option 3): Separated by the Sunda Strait, in Indonesia — outside Indian waters altogether.

 

• The Amindivi and the Laccadive groups (Option 4): Both are parts of Lakshadweep, and the channel dividing Lakshadweep from Minicoy is the Nine Degree Channel.

question: The total length of India's coastline, including the coastlines of its islands, is approximately _____.
solution_text:
The correct answer is 7,516 km.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• India's total coastline, including the island territories, is about 7,516.6 km. (भारत की तटरेखा — लगभग 7,516 किमी)

 

• Of this, the mainland coastline — from Gujarat to West Bengal — is about 6,100 km, and the remainder belongs to the Andaman & Nicobar and Lakshadweep islands.

 

• Gujarat has the longest coastline of any Indian state, followed by Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu.

 

• Nine states and four union territories have a coast: Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha and West Bengal, with Daman & Diu, Dadra & Nagar Haveli, Puducherry, Lakshadweep and the Andaman & Nicobar Islands.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Figures about India worth memorising together:

 

• Area – 32,87,263 sq km, or about 3.28 million sq km; the seventh largest country

 

• Coastline – 7,516.6 km in all

 

• Land frontier – 15,200 km

 

• North-south extent – 3,214 km; east-west – 2,933 km

 

• India shares its land border with seven countries: Bangladesh (the longest), China, Pakistan, Nepal, Myanmar, Bhutan and Afghanistan.

 

NOTE

 

• 5,422 km (Option 1): Less than even the mainland coastline, and not a figure that corresponds to any standard measurement.

 

• 9,240 km (Option 3): Considerably more than the accepted figure.

 

• 6,100 km (Option 4): The approximate length of the mainland coastline alone, excluding the islands. This is the strongest distractor, and the question turns precisely on whether the islands are counted.

question: The Ashokan pillar at Sarnath, whose capital was adopted as India's State Emblem, was carved from stone quarried at _____.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Chunar.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Ashokan pillars, including the one at Sarnath, were carved from the fine-grained buff sandstone quarried at CHUNAR, near Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh, on the bank of the Ganga. (चुनार — अशोक स्तंभों का पत्थर)

 

• The choice of a single quarry for pillars set up across the empire is itself significant: the finished shafts, some weighing fifty tonnes, were transported hundreds of kilometres by river and road.

 

• The Sarnath Lion Capital shows four Asiatic lions standing back to back on an abacus carrying four animals — the lion, elephant, bull and horse — separated by four wheels, above an inverted lotus.

 

• It was adopted as the State Emblem of India on 26 January 1950. In the emblem only three lions are visible, the fourth being hidden from view; the bull and the horse appear on the abacus, and the words "Satyameva Jayate", from the Mundaka Upanishad, are inscribed below in Devanagari.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The polish on the Ashokan pillars — the so-called "Mauryan polish" — is so fine that early visitors took the stone for metal, and the technique has never been satisfactorily explained.

 

• The Ashoka Chakra on the national flag is the wheel from the Sarnath capital, with 24 spokes.

 

• Sarnath itself is where the Buddha preached his first sermon, the *Dhammachakra Pravartana*.

 

NOTE

 

• Mathura (Option 2): The source of the red spotted sandstone used by the Kushana and later sculptors, and the name of a great school of ancient Indian art. The colour alone distinguishes it from Chunar stone.

 

• Makrana (Option 3): In Rajasthan, the source of the white marble used for the Taj Mahal and the Dilwara temples.

 

• Karauli (Option 4): In Rajasthan, the source of the red sandstone used in the Red Fort and in much of Mughal Delhi.

question: Which Article of the Constitution empowers Parliament to legislate on a subject in the State List in the national interest, if the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution supported by two-thirds of the members present and voting?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Article 249.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• ARTICLE 249 empowers Parliament to legislate on a State List subject in the national interest, provided the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution to that effect supported by two-thirds of the members present and voting. (अनुच्छेद 249)

 

• Two features of the provision are worth noting, and both are examined:

 

• The resolution must be passed by the RAJYA SABHA, and by no other House — a recognition of its character as the chamber representing the States.

 

• Such a resolution remains in force for one year, and may be renewed any number of times for a year at a time. A law made under it ceases to have effect six months after the resolution expires.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The five circumstances in which Parliament may legislate on the State List:

 

• Article 249 – the Rajya Sabha so resolves, in the national interest

 

• Article 250 – a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation

 

• Article 252 – two or more States request it; the law then applies to those States, and to any other that adopts it

 

• Article 253 – to give effect to an international agreement

 

• Article 356 – during President's Rule in a State

 

• India's federal scheme is contained in the Seventh Schedule, with the Union List (97 subjects), the State List (66) and the Concurrent List (47). Residuary powers rest with Parliament under Article 248.

 

NOTE

 

• Article 248 (Option 1): Deals with residuary powers — matters mentioned in none of the three lists — which belong to Parliament.

 

• Article 252 (Option 3): Applies where two or more State legislatures pass resolutions requesting Parliament to legislate. It has been used for laws such as the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act.

 

• Article 253 (Option 4): Empowers Parliament to legislate on any subject whatever to give effect to an international treaty or convention — the basis of much of India's environmental legislation.

question: "Charkula", in which women dance balancing a large multi-tiered lamp-stand on the head, belongs to which region?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Braj (western Uttar Pradesh).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Charkula is the folk dance of the BRAJ region of western Uttar Pradesh — the country around Mathura and Vrindavan associated with Krishna. (चरकुला — ब्रज क्षेत्र)

 

• Its distinguishing feature is the Charkula itself: a large wooden pyramid of several tiers, carrying as many as 108 oil lamps, which the dancer balances on her head while she dances.

 

• The dancers are veiled, and the dance is performed to the singing of Rasiya songs.

 

• It is danced chiefly on the third day after Holi, and by tradition commemorates the moment when Radha's grandmother carried out a lamp-stand to announce her birth.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other folk forms of Uttar Pradesh: Raslila and Charkula in Braj; Nautanki, the great folk theatre; Kajri, the song of the rains; Chaiti, Birha and Khyal.

 

• Dances performed with something balanced on the head are found across India, and are worth grouping: Charkula (a lamp-stand, Braj), Bhavai (pots, Rajasthan), Karagattam (a pot, Tamil Nadu), Hojagiri (bottles and lamps on pitchers, Tripura) and Matki (a pot, Madhya Pradesh).

 

NOTE

 

• Bundelkhand (Option 1): The region of southern Uttar Pradesh and northern Madhya Pradesh, known for the heroic ballad Alha and for the Rai dance.

 

• Malwa (Option 2): The plateau of western Madhya Pradesh, known for Matki, Grida and the Malwi Lok Geet.

 

• Rohilkhand (Option 4): The region around Bareilly in northern Uttar Pradesh, named after the Rohillas, with no dance of this kind.

question: Animal tissues are classified into how many main types?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 4.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Animal tissues are classified into FOUR main types. (जंतु ऊतक — चार प्रकार)

 

• EPITHELIAL tissue – covers the surfaces of the body and lines its cavities and organs; it protects, absorbs and secretes. The skin, the lining of the mouth and of the blood vessels are all epithelial.

 

• CONNECTIVE tissue – binds and supports the other tissues. It includes bone, cartilage, blood, lymph, tendons, ligaments and adipose (fat) tissue. Blood is a connective tissue, which is the point most often missed.

 

• MUSCULAR tissue – brings about movement; of three kinds — striated (skeletal), smooth (involuntary) and cardiac.

 

• NERVOUS tissue – conducts impulses; made of neurons, the longest cells in the body.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Plant tissues, by contrast, are classified first into two groups:

 

• MERISTEMATIC – capable of division; of three kinds: apical (at the tips of root and shoot, increasing length), lateral (increasing girth) and intercalary (at the base of leaves and internodes)

 

• PERMANENT – which have lost the power of division. Simple: parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma. Complex: xylem and phloem.

 

NOTE

 

• 3 (Option 1): The number of kinds of meristematic tissue in plants, and of muscular tissue in animals — a figure that belongs to a sub-classification, not to the main one.

 

• 5 (Option 3): No standard classification of animal tissue gives five main types.

 

• 6 (Option 4): Again not a standard figure. Some texts subdivide connective tissue further, but the main classification remains four.

question: The "Hemis Festival", held at a monastery in honour of Guru Padmasambhava, is celebrated in which union territory?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Ladakh.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Hemis Festival is held at the Hemis Monastery, about 45 km from Leh, in the union territory of LADAKH. (हेमिस उत्सव — लद्दाख)

 

• It is celebrated in June or July, on the tenth day of the Tibetan lunar month, in honour of the birth of Guru Padmasambhava — the eighth-century teacher who carried Buddhism to Tibet, and who is revered as Guru Rinpoche.

 

• Its central event is the Chham, the masked dance performed by the lamas in the monastery courtyard, in which the victory of good over evil is enacted.

 

• Hemis is the largest and wealthiest monastery in Ladakh, belonging to the Drukpa order and founded in 1630. Once every twelve years, in the Year of the Monkey, its great thangka — an embroidered silk scroll — is unfurled for public view.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Ladakh became a union territory on 31 October 2019, when Jammu and Kashmir was reorganised. It has two districts — Leh and Kargil — and no legislature.

 

• Other festivals of Ladakh: Losar (the new year, held early in Ladakh), Sindhu Darshan at Leh in June, Dosmoche, Yuru Kabgyat and the Ladakh Harvest Festival.

 

NOTE

 

• Jammu and Kashmir (Option 2): The union territory from which Ladakh was separated in 2019, and the answer most candidates give from habit. Its own festivals are the Tulip Festival at Srinagar and the Shikara Festival on the Dal Lake.

 

• Sikkim (Option 3): Its Buddhist festivals are Losoong, Saga Dawa and Pang Lhabsol, and its monasteries are Rumtek and Pemayangtse. It is a state, not a union territory.

 

• Himachal Pradesh (Option 4): Also a state. Its festivals are the Kullu Dussehra, Losar in Lahaul-Spiti, and the Minjar Fair at Chamba.

question: According to the Census of 2011, which union territory recorded the highest literacy rate?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Lakshadweep.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• According to the Census of 2011, LAKSHADWEEP recorded the highest literacy rate of any union territory, at about 91.85 per cent. (लक्षद्वीप — केंद्रशासित प्रदेशों में सर्वाधिक साक्षरता)

 

• It stood second in India as a whole, behind Kerala (93.91%) and ahead of Mizoram (91.33%).

 

• Lakshadweep also recorded the highest male literacy rate in India, at about 96.11 per cent.

 

• Among the union territories the order was Lakshadweep, Delhi (86.21%), Chandigarh (86.05%) and Puducherry (85.85%).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Literacy figures from the Census of 2011:

 

• All-India literacy – 74.04%; male 82.14%, female 65.46%

 

• Highest state – Kerala (93.91%); lowest – Bihar (63.82%)

 

• Highest female literacy – Kerala; highest male literacy – Lakshadweep

 

• Lakshadweep is India's smallest union territory by area — 32 sq km — and consists of 36 islands, of which only 10 are inhabited. Its capital is Kavaratti, and its language is Malayalam, except on Minicoy, where Mahl is spoken.

 

NOTE

 

• Delhi (Option 1): Recorded 86.21%, the second highest among the union territories, and it is the answer most candidates give because of its size and prominence.

 

• Puducherry (Option 3): Recorded 85.85%, the lowest of the four listed here.

 

• Chandigarh (Option 4): Recorded 86.05%, very close behind Delhi.

question: A passenger standing in a stationary bus falls backwards when the bus starts suddenly. This happens because of _____.
solution_text:
The correct answer is inertia of rest.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A passenger falls backwards when a stationary bus starts suddenly because of the INERTIA OF REST. (विराम का जड़त्व)

 

• The reason is worth setting out exactly. The feet of the passenger are in contact with the floor and move forward at once with the bus. The upper part of his body, having no such contact, tends to remain at rest. The lower body therefore moves forward while the upper body stays behind, and he falls backwards.

 

• The same principle explains why a passenger lurches forward when a moving bus stops suddenly — but that is the inertia of MOTION, and the two must not be confused.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The three kinds of inertia, with an example of each:

 

• INERTIA OF REST – a body at rest tends to stay at rest. *Dust flies off a carpet when it is beaten; the coin drops into the glass when the card beneath it is flicked away; the passenger falls backward when the bus starts.*

 

• INERTIA OF MOTION – a body in motion tends to stay in motion. *A passenger lurches forward when the bus brakes; an athlete runs some distance past the finishing line; a man jumping from a moving train falls forward.*

 

• INERTIA OF DIRECTION – a body tends to keep moving in the same direction. *Mud flies off a turning wheel along the tangent; a passenger leans outward when the bus takes a sharp turn.*

 

• Inertia is the subject of Newton's First Law, which is for that reason called the law of inertia. The mass of a body is the measure of its inertia.

 

NOTE

 

• inertia of motion (Option 1): Explains the opposite case — falling forward when a moving vehicle stops suddenly. This is the principal trap in the question.

 

• inertia of direction (Option 3): Explains what happens at a turn, not at a start or a stop.

 

• centrifugal force (Option 4): The apparent outward force felt by a body moving in a circle. It has no application to motion in a straight line, and is in any case a fictitious force arising from the observer's own rotation.

question: "Tiranga Point" on the Moon marks the site associated with which Indian mission?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Chandrayaan-2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Tiranga Point" is the name given to the point on the lunar surface associated with CHANDRAYAAN-2, whose lander Vikram made a hard landing in September 2019. (तिरंगा प्वाइंट — चंद्रयान-2)

 

• The name was announced by the Prime Minister in August 2023, at the same time as the naming of "Shiv Shakti Point", the successful landing site of Chandrayaan-3.

 

• Chandrayaan-2 was not a failure in the ordinary sense. Its orbiter continues to function, and has returned a great deal of data; only the lander and the rover were lost.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• India's lunar missions:

 

• Chandrayaan-1 (2008) – the first; its Moon Impact Probe carried the Indian flag to the surface, and the mission found evidence of water molecules on the Moon

 

• Chandrayaan-2 (2019) – orbiter successful; lander Vikram lost. Site named Tiranga Point

 

• Chandrayaan-3 (2023) – landed successfully near the lunar south pole on 23 August 2023, making India the fourth country to soft-land on the Moon and the first to reach the south polar region. Site named Shiv Shakti Point

 

• 23 August is now observed every year as National Space Day.

 

NOTE

 

• Chandrayaan-1 (Option 2): India's first lunar mission, launched in 2008. It carried an impact probe rather than a lander, and no landing site of its own was named.

 

• Chandrayaan-3 (Option 3): The successful mission, whose landing site was named Shiv Shakti Point — announced on the same occasion, which is exactly why the two are confused.

 

• Mangalyaan (Option 4): The Mars Orbiter Mission of 2013. It never approached the Moon at all.

question: According to the Census of 2011, which state has the highest proportion of Scheduled Tribe population?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Mizoram.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• According to the Census of 2011, MIZORAM has the highest proportion of Scheduled Tribe population of any state, at about 94.4 per cent. (मिजोरम — सर्वाधिक अनुसूचित जनजाति अनुपात)

 

• The order among the states is Mizoram (94.4%), Nagaland (86.5%), Meghalaya (86.1%) and Arunachal Pradesh (68.8%).

 

• Two distinctions must be kept apart, and the question turns on the first:

 

• Highest PROPORTION of ST population – Mizoram among the states, and Lakshadweep (94.8%) among all units

 

• Largest NUMBER of tribal people – Madhya Pradesh, followed by Maharashtra and Odisha

 

• India's Scheduled Tribe population in 2011 was about 10.43 crore, or 8.6 per cent of the total.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Punjab, Haryana, Delhi, Puducherry and Chandigarh have no notified Scheduled Tribes at all.

 

• Article 342 empowers the President to specify the tribes or tribal communities to be deemed Scheduled Tribes in relation to each State or Union Territory, after consultation with the Governor.

 

• The National Commission for Scheduled Tribes was constituted under Article 338A, by the 89th Constitutional Amendment (2003), which separated it from the Commission for Scheduled Castes.

 

• Janjatiya Gaurav Divas is observed on 15 November, the birth anniversary of Birsa Munda.

 

NOTE

 

• Nagaland (Option 1): Second, at about 86.5 per cent — very close behind, which makes it the strongest distractor.

 

• Meghalaya (Option 2): Third, at about 86.1 per cent. Its principal communities are the Khasi, Garo and Jaintia, all of them matrilineal.

 

• Arunachal Pradesh (Option 4): About 68.8 per cent, and home to 26 major tribes — the greatest variety of tribal communities of any state, though not the highest proportion.

question: The James Webb Space Telescope, launched in December 2021, is a joint project of NASA with which two agencies?
solution_text:
The correct answer is ESA and CSA.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) is a joint project of NASA with the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Canadian Space Agency (CSA). (जेम्स वेब स्पेस टेलीस्कोप)

 

• It was launched on 25 December 2021 on an Ariane 5 rocket from Kourou in French Guiana — the launch itself being ESA's contribution.

 

• It is stationed at the second Lagrange point (L2), about 1.5 million km from the Earth on the side away from the Sun, where it keeps station with the Earth as both orbit the Sun.

 

• Its primary mirror is 6.5 metres across, made of eighteen hexagonal gold-coated beryllium segments that unfolded after launch.

 

• It observes chiefly in the infrared, which allows it to see through dust and to detect the most distant and earliest galaxies, whose light has been red-shifted out of the visible range.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• JWST is the successor to the Hubble Space Telescope, and the difference between them is worth knowing:

 

• Hubble (1990) – orbits the Earth at about 550 km; observes chiefly in visible and ultraviolet light; has been serviced by astronauts

 

• JWST (2021) – stationed at L2, far beyond reach of repair; observes in the infrared; has a mirror nearly three times the diameter

 

• India's own space observatory is AstroSat, launched in 2015, and Aditya-L1, launched in 2023 to study the Sun from the first Lagrange point.

 

NOTE

 

• JAXA and ISRO (Option 1): The Japanese and Indian agencies. India's collaboration with JAXA concerns the proposed LUPEX lunar mission, not JWST.

 

• Roscosmos and CNSA (Option 3): The Russian and Chinese agencies, neither of which took part.

 

• ESA and JAXA (Option 4): The strongest distractor, since ESA is indeed a partner. But the third partner is Canada, not Japan — Canada supplied the Fine Guidance Sensor and the NIRISS instrument.

question: The Chota Nagpur Plateau, often called the mineral heartland of India, lies mainly in which state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Jharkhand.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Chota Nagpur Plateau lies mainly in JHARKHAND, extending into the neighbouring parts of Odisha, West Bengal, Bihar and Chhattisgarh. (छोटा नागपुर पठार — झारखंड)

 

• It is called the "mineral heartland of India" because it holds the country's richest concentration of coal, iron ore, mica, bauxite, copper, limestone and uranium.

 

• Its principal fields and deposits:

 

• Coal – Jharia, Bokaro, Giridih, Karanpura

 

• Iron ore – Noamundi, Gua

 

• Copper – Ghatsila (Singhbhum)

 

• Uranium – Jaduguda, India's first uranium mine

 

• Mica – the Kodarma belt, once the largest producer in the world

 

• The plateau is made of very old Gondwana rock, and is drained by the Damodar, the Subarnarekha and the North Koel.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Damodar valley, running through the plateau, was the site of India's first multipurpose river valley project — the Damodar Valley Corporation (1948), modelled on the Tennessee Valley Authority. The Damodar was called the "Sorrow of Bengal" before it was controlled.

 

• The proximity of coal and iron ore explains the siting of India's steel industry: Jamshedpur, Bokaro, Rourkela, Durgapur and Bhilai all lie on or near the plateau.

 

NOTE

 

• Odisha (Option 2): Holds the eastern extension of the plateau, and is India's largest producer of iron ore — which makes it a genuine distractor. But the plateau's core lies in Jharkhand.

 

• Chhattisgarh (Option 3): Holds the Bastar and Dalli-Rajhara deposits, on the Baghelkhand and Dandakaranya plateaus rather than Chota Nagpur.

 

• West Bengal (Option 4): Holds the western fringe of the plateau, including the Raniganj coalfield — the oldest in India, worked since 1774.

question: The headquarters of the World Trade Organization is located in _____.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Geneva.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The World Trade Organization (WTO) has its headquarters at GENEVA, Switzerland. (विश्व व्यापार संगठन — जिनेवा)

 

• It was established on 1 January 1995, replacing the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) of 1948, at the end of the Uruguay Round of negotiations.

 

• India is a founder member, having also been a founder member of GATT.

 

• Its highest decision-making body is the Ministerial Conference, which meets at least once every two years, and decisions are ordinarily taken by consensus rather than by vote.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• International organisations headquartered at GENEVA — an unusually long list, and one worth learning as a block:

 

• WTO, WHO, ILO, WIPO, WMO, ITU, UNHCR, UNCTAD, the International Committee of the Red Cross, and the European Organization for Nuclear Research (CERN) nearby

 

• Elsewhere: UN and UNICEF – New York; UNESCO – Paris; IMF and World Bank – Washington DC; FAO and IFAD – Rome; IAEA and OPEC – Vienna; ICJ – The Hague; ADB – Manila; AIIB – Beijing; NDB – Shanghai.

 

NOTE

 

• New York (Option 2): Headquarters of the United Nations itself and of UNICEF, which is why it is the answer most often guessed.

 

• Paris (Option 3): Headquarters of UNESCO, the OECD and the Financial Action Task Force (FATF).

 

• Vienna (Option 4): Headquarters of the IAEA, OPEC, UNIDO and the CTBTO.

question: The Competition Commission of India was established under which enactment?
solution_text:
The correct answer is The Competition Act, 2002.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Competition Commission of India (CCI) was established under the COMPETITION ACT, 2002, and began functioning fully in 2009. Its headquarters is at New Delhi. (भारतीय प्रतिस्पर्धा आयोग — प्रतिस्पर्धा अधिनियम, 2002)

 

• It replaced the MRTP Commission, set up under the Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices Act of 1969, which was repealed.

 

• The change of approach is the point worth grasping. The MRTP Act was directed against size — it treated large concentrations of economic power as objectionable in themselves. The Competition Act is directed against conduct — it treats size as unobjectionable and penalises the abuse of a dominant position.

 

• The CCI's three principal functions are to prohibit anti-competitive agreements, to prevent the abuse of dominance, and to regulate combinations — mergers and acquisitions above a stated threshold.

 

• Appeals from its orders lie to the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Act followed the report of the Raghavan Committee (1999) on competition policy and law, appointed as part of the reform of the economic legislation of the pre-liberalisation era.

 

• A cartel — an agreement among competitors to fix prices or share markets — is treated by the Act as presumptively anti-competitive, and the CCI operates a leniency programme under which the first member of a cartel to disclose it may receive a reduced penalty.

 

NOTE

 

• The MRTP Act, 1969 (Option 2): The predecessor legislation, which the Competition Act repealed. It is the strongest distractor, and the distinction between the two Acts is the substance of the question.

 

• The Companies Act, 2013 (Option 3): Governs the incorporation and management of companies, and established the NCLT and the NFRA — not the CCI.

 

• FEMA, 1999 (Option 4): The Foreign Exchange Management Act, which replaced FERA and governs foreign exchange transactions.

question: Who is the author of the novel "Em and the Big Hoom"?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Jerry Pinto.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Em and the Big Hoom" (2012) was written by Jerry Pinto, and was his first novel. (एम एंड द बिग हूम — जेरी पिंटो)

 

• It is set in a one-bedroom flat in Mahim, Bombay, and is narrated by a son whose mother — called Em — suffers from bipolar disorder. The Big Hoom is his father.

 

• It is regarded as one of the few Indian novels to treat mental illness within a family without sentiment and without evasion, and it draws on the author's own experience.

 

• It won the Sahitya Akademi Award for English in 2016, the Hindu Literary Prize (2013) and the Windham-Campbell Prize (2016).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Jerry Pinto is also a poet, a journalist and a translator from Marathi, and wrote "Helen: The Life and Times of an H-Bomb", a study of the film dancer, which won a National Film Award.

 

• Novels of Bombay worth knowing together: *Em and the Big Hoom* (Jerry Pinto), *Maximum City* (Suketu Mehta, non-fiction), *Shantaram* (Gregory David Roberts), *Such a Long Journey* (Rohinton Mistry), *Ravan and Eddie* (Kiran Nagarkar) and *Last Man in Tower* (Aravind Adiga).

 

NOTE

 

• Amit Chaudhuri (Option 1): Novelist, essayist and musician, author of "A Strange and Sublime Address", "Afternoon Raag" and "Freedom Song", and a writer chiefly of Calcutta.

 

• Rohinton Mistry (Option 2): Author of "Such a Long Journey", "A Fine Balance" and "Family Matters", three times shortlisted for the Booker Prize.

 

• Cyrus Mistry (Option 3): Author of "Chronicle of a Corpse Bearer", which won the DSC Prize for South Asian Literature in 2014. He was the younger brother of Rohinton Mistry.

question: In cricket, the fielding position square of the wicket on the off side, close to the batter, is called _____.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Point.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• POINT is the fielding position square of the wicket on the off side, standing close to the batter — that is, roughly at right angles to the line between the two sets of stumps. (प्वाइंट — क्षेत्ररक्षण की स्थिति)

 

• The name is said to come from the older phrase *"the point of the bat"*, the fielder being stationed level with the point at which the batter's bat comes down.

 

• The off-side positions, moving round from square towards the bowler, are: point → cover point → cover → extra cover → mid-off.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The principal fielding positions:

 

• Off side, close: slip, gully, point, silly point

 

• Off side, in front: cover, extra cover, mid-off

 

• Leg side, close: leg slip, short leg, square leg

 

• Leg side, in front: mid-on, mid-wicket

 

• Behind, on the boundary: third man (off), fine leg (leg), long on, long off, deep square leg

 

• The off side is the side the batter faces; the leg (or on) side is behind him. The sides therefore change when a left-handed batter takes strike, which is why the field is reset between batters.

 

• A team may have no more than two fielders behind square on the leg side, a restriction introduced after the Bodyline series of 1932-33.

 

NOTE

 

• Gully (Option 1): Stands between the slips and point, and is therefore behind square rather than square of the wicket.

 

• Cover (Option 3): Stands in front of square on the off side, between point and mid-off — further round towards the bowler.

 

• Mid-off (Option 4): Stands near the bowler on the off side, almost straight down the pitch, and is the furthest of the four from square.

question: In basketball, a successful shot taken from beyond the arc is worth how many points?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In basketball, a successful shot taken from beyond the three-point arc is worth THREE points. (बास्केटबॉल — तीन अंक)

 

• The scoring is on three levels:

 

• 3 points – a field goal from beyond the arc

 

• 2 points – a field goal from inside the arc

 

• 1 point – a successful free throw

 

• Under the rules of FIBA, which govern international and Olympic basketball, the arc is 6.75 metres from the basket.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The essentials of basketball:

 

• Five players a side on the court, with seven substitutes permitted

 

• Four quarters of 10 minutes each under FIBA rules

 

• The basket is 10 feet (3.05 m) above the floor

 

• The court measures 28 m by 15 m

 

• The shot clock allows 24 seconds to attempt a shot

 

• The game was invented in 1891 by James Naismith, a Canadian physical education instructor in Massachusetts, who nailed two peach baskets to a gallery rail. It entered the Olympics in 1936 at Berlin.

 

• India's governing body is the Basketball Federation of India, and Satnam Singh Bhamara was the first Indian to be drafted by the NBA, in 2015.

 

NOTE

 

• 2 (Option 1): The value of a field goal from inside the arc — much the commonest score in a match, and the answer most often given.

 

• 4 (Option 2): No shot in basketball is worth four points. A four-point play occurs only when a three-point shot is scored and a foul awarded, giving a free throw in addition.

 

• 1 (Option 4): The value of a free throw, awarded after a foul.

question: The construction of the Taj Mahal at Agra took approximately how many years to complete?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 22.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Taj Mahal took approximately 22 years to build — from about 1632 to 1653. (ताजमहल — लगभग 22 वर्ष)

 

• It was built by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died in 1631 at Burhanpur while giving birth to their fourteenth child.

 

• Some twenty thousand workmen are said to have been employed, and the chief architect is generally identified as Ustad Ahmad Lahauri.

 

• The white marble came from Makrana in Rajasthan, and the inlaid stones from as far as Afghanistan, Tibet, Sri Lanka and Arabia.

 

• It stands on the bank of the Yamuna, and was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983 — among the first four Indian sites to be listed.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The building is the finest example of the Mughal charbagh plan — a garden divided into four quarters by water channels, representing the gardens of paradise. Unusually, the tomb stands at the end of the garden rather than at its centre.

 

• Its decorative technique is pietra dura — the inlay of coloured semi-precious stones in marble — and the calligraphy is by Amanat Khan.

 

• Shah Jahan's other works: the Red Fort and the Jama Masjid at Delhi, the Moti Masjid at Agra, and the city of Shahjahanabad. His reign is called the Golden Age of Mughal architecture.

 

NOTE

 

• 12 (Option 1): Too short. The main mausoleum alone is thought to have taken about twelve years, but the complex — the mosque, the guest house, the gateway and the garden — took a decade more.

 

• 30 (Option 2): Too long. Shah Jahan was deposed by Aurangzeb in 1658, five years after the work was finished.

 

• 40 (Option 4): Far too long, and would carry the construction well into Aurangzeb's reign.

question: Which of the following is a "Ghana Vadya" — a solid instrument that produces sound without needing to be tuned?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Manjira.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The MANJIRA — a pair of small metal cymbals struck against each other — is a GHANA VADYA, or solid instrument. (मंजीरा — घन वाद्य)

 

• A Ghana Vadya is made of a solid material — metal, wood or stone — that vibrates as a whole when struck. Such instruments need no tuning, which is what distinguishes them from every other class.

 

• The manjira accompanies bhajans, kirtans and folk music throughout India, and keeps the *tala*.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The four classes of Indian musical instrument, as set out in Bharata's Natyashastra — a classification about two thousand years old, and one that anticipates the modern Hornbostel-Sachs system:

 

• TATA VADYA – string: sitar, sarod, veena, sarangi, santoor, violin

 

• SUSHIRA VADYA – wind: bansuri, shehnai, nadaswaram, pungi, bargu

 

• AVANADDHA VADYA – membrane: tabla, mridangam, pakhawaj, dhol, chenda

 

• GHANA VADYA – solid: manjira, jhanj, ghatam, morsing, jaltarang, khartal

 

• The ghatam, an earthen pot used in Carnatic music, and the jaltarang, a set of tuned porcelain bowls, are the two Ghana Vadya instruments most often given concert status.

 

NOTE

 

• Sarangi (Option 1): A bowed string instrument — Tata Vadya — stopped with the fingernails, and held to come closest to the human voice.

 

• Shehnai (Option 3): A double-reed wind instrument — Sushira Vadya — made famous by Ustad Bismillah Khan.

 

• Mridangam (Option 4): The principal percussion instrument of Carnatic music, with a stretched membrane at each end — Avanaddha Vadya. It is the closest distractor, since both it and the manjira mark rhythm, but the mridangam has a skin and must be tuned.

question: Which newspaper was founded by Mahatma Gandhi in South Africa in 1903?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Indian Opinion.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Indian Opinion" was founded by Mahatma Gandhi in 1903 at Durban, South Africa. (इंडियन ओपिनियन — 1903)

 

• It was published in English and Gujarati, and at first also in Hindi and Tamil, and it was the voice of the Indian community's struggle against discriminatory legislation.

 

• It was later printed at the Phoenix Settlement near Durban, the community Gandhi founded in 1904 after reading Ruskin's "Unto This Last" — a book he afterwards paraphrased into Gujarati as *Sarvodaya*.

 

• Gandhi refused to accept advertisements for it, holding that a journal dependent on advertisers could not be independent — a principle he kept for every paper he afterwards edited.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Gandhi's newspapers, in order:

 

• Indian Opinion – 1903, South Africa; English and Gujarati

 

• Young India – 1919-1931, in English, taken over from Indulal Yagnik

 

• Navajivan – 1919, in Gujarati, later also in Hindi

 

• Harijan – 1933, in English, with Harijan Bandhu in Gujarati and Harijan Sevak in Hindi

 

• It was in Young India that Gandhi published his article *"Shaking the Manes"*, and in Harijan that he wrote chiefly on untouchability and village industry.

 

NOTE

 

• Young India (Option 1): Taken up by Gandhi in 1919 in India, and the paper in which he wrote the articles for which he was tried for sedition in 1922.

 

• Navajivan (Option 3): The Gujarati weekly he began in 1919, in which *The Story of My Experiments with Truth* was first serialised from 1925.

 

• Harijan (Option 4): Founded in 1933, after Gandhi's fast and the Poona Pact, and devoted chiefly to the removal of untouchability. It is the latest of the four.
